overview:
Nauru is a single oval island in the Pacific Ocean, just south of the equator and about 300 kilometers from its nearest neighbor. At 21 km² it is the smallest republic on Earth and the third-smallest country of any kind, after Vatican City and Monaco. A person can drive all the way around it on the coast road in about half an hour.

Roughly 12,000 people live on Nauru, almost all of them in a narrow ring of villages between the beach and the cliffs. English and Nauruan are the official languages. Nauru has no official capital city in the usual sense; government offices sit in the district of Yaren, which is listed as the capital. The country is a republic with an elected parliament of 19 members.

For a few decades Nauru was extraordinarily rich from mining phosphate rock, then the money and much of the island's interior ran out.
landAndNature: A flat coastal strip of coconut palms and pandanus trees rings the island, rising to a limestone plateau Nauruans call Topside. That plateau was once thick with phosphate, a mineral made from ancient seabird droppings piled up over millions of years and prized as fertilizer. Mining stripped away the soil and left a moonscape of jagged coral pinnacles across about four-fifths of the interior. Buada Lagoon, a brackish pond ringed by trees, is the island's only sizable body of fresh-ish water. Offshore, coral reefs drop away steeply into deep ocean, and frigatebirds and noddies wheel above. Nauru gets steady sun, heavy tropical downpours, and droughts that can last months.
peopleAndCulture: Nauruans trace descent through twelve traditional clans, and the country's flag shows a twelve-pointed star for them. Families are close, feasts are large, and fish, coconut and rice are everyday foods, though imported canned and packaged food became common during the mining years. A striking old tradition is frigatebird catching: young birds are lured in, tamed and kept, then sometimes released to return home. Angam Day on October 26 marks the moment in 1932 when the Nauruan population recovered to 1,500 after disease and war had nearly wiped it out. Australian rules football and weightlifting are the favorite sports, and Nauru has won Commonwealth Games gold medals in weightlifting.
history: Micronesian and Polynesian voyagers settled Nauru at least 3,000 years ago. A British whaling captain sighted it in 1798 and named it Pleasant Island. Germany annexed Nauru in 1888, and phosphate was discovered in 1900. Australia, Britain and New Zealand mined it under a League of Nations mandate; Japan occupied the island during World War II and deported more than 1,200 Nauruans to Chuuk, where many died. Nauru became independent on January 31, 1968, bought out the mining company and, briefly, had one of the world's highest incomes per person. Bad investments and exhausted phosphate left the country nearly bankrupt by 2000. Since 2001 Nauru has earned much of its income by hosting an Australian offshore center for asylum seekers, an arrangement widely criticized by human rights groups.
funFacts: Nauru has no army, no rivers, and for many years no capital city in the ordinary sense.
The country once ran an airline with a single plane; when it needed repairs, the whole nation's air service stopped.
Nauru's phosphate began as seabird droppings, called guano, that built up on coral over millions of years.
The island's ring road is about 19 kilometers long, and driving it takes roughly 20 to 30 minutes.
Nauru was the smallest country ever to compete at the Olympic Games when it debuted in 1996.
